Anti-inflammatory medications are drugs that are used to reduce inflammation, swelling, and redness in the body. Inflammation is a natural response of the body to injury or infection, and it is characterized by swelling, pain, redness, and warmth. Anti-inflammatory medications work by blocking the production of substances that cause inflammation, or by inhibiting the action of these substances. There are many different types of anti-inflammatory medications, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroids.NSAIDs are a type of anti-inflammatory medication that is commonly used to reduce inflammation, swelling, and pain. Examples of NSAIDs include ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin. These medications work by blocking the production of prostaglandins, which are chemicals that contribute to inflammation. NSAIDs are often used to treat conditions such as arthritis, sprains, and muscle strains. Corticosteroids are another type of anti-inflammatory medication that is used to reduce inflammation. These medications are more potent than NSAIDs and are often used to treat more severe cases of inflammation. Corticosteroids are available in oral, topical, and injectable forms and are commonly used to treat conditions such as asthma, allergies, and inflammatory bowel disease. It is important to note that anti-inflammatory medications can have side effects, and they may not be suitable for everyone. It is important to speak with a healthcare provider before starting any new medication to discuss the potential risks and benefits.

It can make sense to sell a stock and then repurchase it for tax purposes, depending on your individual circumstances and financial goals. This strategy, known as tax-loss harvesting, involves selling a security that has decreased in value in order to realize a capital loss, which can then be used to offset capital gains from other investments or to reduce your overall tax bill. There are a few things to consider when using tax-loss harvesting as a strategy: You need to ensure that you have a capital gain to offset. If you don't have any capital gains, you won't be able to use the capital loss to reduce your tax liability. You need to be aware of the wash-sale rule, which prohibits you from claiming a loss on a security if you repurchase the same security (or a substantially similar security) within 30 days of the sale. If you do repurchase the security within this time frame, the loss will be disallowed for tax purposes. You should also consider the opportunity cost of selling and repurchasing the stock. If you believe that the stock will continue to increase in value, you may be sacrificing potential gains by selling it. Overall, tax-loss harvesting can be a useful strategy for reducing your tax liability, but it's important to carefully consider your individual circumstances and financial goals before making any investment decisions.

Now, you might be wondering why NASA doesn't just launch from a really high mountain, like in the Rockies. While it's true that a higher altitude would give the rocket a bit of a boost, it's not enough to make a big difference. Plus, launching from a mountain would also mean that the rocket would have to fly through a lot more air, which would cause it to slow down and use more fuel. Overall, it's just easier and more efficient to launch rockets from a location that is close to the equator, like Kennedy Space Center in Florida or the Guiana Space Centre in South America.

Consider putting a baseball in boiling water. As soon as you put it in, the outside of the baseball is immediately at 212F/100C. The same thing is happening with deep fried ice cream in terms of the ice cream melting. Now, the deep fried ice cream has two advantages over the baseball-it has a layer of batter outside that's the only part that actually need to get fried; and it's frozen at an extra cold temperature to begin with. So you throw it in, the batter on the outside gets hot and cooks almost instantly, and the inside is still cold. Imagine this: We shoot video of a metronome. It's making exactly 10 clicks per second, no more and no less. We shoot ten minutes of this video. When we play the video back, we hear 10 clicks per second for ten minutes. Then we adjust the speed of playback so that it is twice as fast. We hear 20 clicks per second for only five minutes. And when we instead play back the video at half of the original speed, we get five clicks per second, for twenty minutes. So we can see that by varying the speed of the playback, we can change how much time passes between events on the screen. All clear so far? Now let's imagine we took that same metronome and sped up the clicks a lot. Now it's sitting there on the table making 440 clicks per second. We can't really hear the distinct clicks anymore-it sounds more like a continuous tone. In fact, it has a pitch-it's an A, even though it's nothing but clicks. Now, if we double the speed of playback, we get 880Hz (Hz, or Hertz, is just clicks per second here). It's another A, but it's an octave above the first A. At half-speed we get 220Hz, which is an A an octave below the first one. So to sum up, sound is actually a lot of very closely spaced events-vibrations, clicks, etc. - and when we speed them up or slow them down, those events are closer together or further apart in time, which changes the pitch.

"Scruffies" use any number of different algorithms and methods to achieve intelligent behavior. Scruffy programs may require large amounts of hand coding or knowledge engineering. Scruffies have argued that the general intelligence can only be implemented by solving a large number of essentially unrelated problems, and that there is no magic bullet that will allow programs to develop general intelligence autonomously. The scruffy approach is more like biology, where much of the work involves studying and categorizing diverse phenomena.[a]

As Lpz said, no, the President isn't powerless. The government is constructed such that there's essentially a three-way Mexican standoff between the three branches of government: the President exists to control Congress and the Supreme Court, Congress exists to control the President and the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court exists to control Congress and the President. As for the exact checks and balances: Executive vs. Legislative: the President can veto Congress' laws, but Congress can override the President's veto with a 2/3 supermajority. Congress can also impeach the President and attempt to remove him from office with a 2/3 supermajority vote. (Only two presidents have so far been impeached, but neither was removed from office.) Judicial vs. Legislative: the Supreme Court can declare laws passed by Congress to be null and void on the basis of unconstitutionality, but Congress decides whether or not a Supreme Court appointee gets the job to begin with. Congress can also impeach Supreme Court justices and attempt to remove them from office with a 2/3 supermajority vote. (Only one Supreme Court justice has so far been impeached, but was not removed from office.) Executive vs. Judicial: the Supreme Court can declare executive orders to be null and void on the basis of unconstitutionality, but the President appoints new Supreme Court justices, who then must be approved by Congress. In short, because any given branch of the government is monitored and limited by the other two, it's easy to conclude that that branch is powerless, when not taking into account the checks and balances poised against its opponents. In theory, this is supposed to encourage laws / executive orders / court rulings that everyone can agree on and therefore make it through the process alive. In practice, it leads to deadlock.

Selective breeding (also called artificial selection) is the process by which humans use animal breeding and plant breeding to selectively develop particular phenotypic traits (characteristics) by choosing which typically animal or plant males and females will sexually reproduce and have offspring together. Domesticated animals are known as breeds, normally bred by a professional breeder, while domesticated plants are known as varieties, cultigens, cultivars, or breeds. Two purebred animals of different breeds produce a crossbreed, and crossbred plants are called hybrids. Flowers, vegetables and fruit-trees may be bred by amateurs and commercial or non-commercial professionals: major crops are usually the provenance of the professionals. In animal breeding, techniques such as inbreeding, linebreeding, and outcrossing are utilized. In plant breeding, similar methods are used. Charles Darwin discussed how selective breeding had been successful in producing change over time in his 1859 book, On the Origin of Species. Its first chapter discusses selective breeding and domestication of such animals as pigeons, cats, cattle, and dogs. Darwin used artificial selection as a springboard to introduce and support the theory of natural selection. The deliberate exploitation of selective breeding to produce desired results has become very common in agriculture and experimental biology. Selective breeding can be unintentional, for example, resulting from the process of human cultivation; and it may also produce unintended - desirable or undesirable - results. For example, in some grains, an increase in seed size may have resulted from certain ploughing practices rather than from the intentional selection of larger seeds. Most likely, there has been an interdependence between natural and artificial factors that have resulted in plant domestication.

A seizure occurs when there is out-of-control electrical activity in your brain. A seizure can take many forms, ranging anywhere from an involuntary muscle twitch, to "blanking out," to losing consciousness and convulsing on ground uncontrollably (which most people think of when they hear the word "seizure"). Seizures can take many forms because they have many causes. They can be focal (i.e. propagating from one area of the brain, such as with a brain tumor or a brain bleed), or can be global (seizure activity everywhere in the brain at once, such as with metabolic disturbances). If you suspect somebody has a seizure, the first diagnostic test to get is an EEG (electroencephalogram), which is essentially an EKG for the brain. It graphs the electrical activity of the brain. A trained neurologist can interpret normal brain wave activity and differentiate it from possible seizure activity. If you are certain that there is seizure activity, you get an MRI to look for any structural abnormalities that can cause seizures (trauma, tumors, AV malformations, etc). Seizures are treated in many different ways. Ideally, you treat the underlying cause (get rid of the tumor, correct the metabolic abnormality, etc), but sometimes this isn't possible. You can also treat them with medications called anti-epileptic drugs. There are many AED's, with different mechanisms of action and different side effects (agitation, suicidal ideations, dizziness, risk of taking when pregnant). Choosing the right AED can be tricky, because you have to know what type of seizure you're treating, and weigh the risk of side effects with the benefit of hopefully stopping the seizures. Almost everyone will have a seizure at some point in their life, and most of us don't remember having one. Needless to say, not everybody is on an AED. We reserve treatment for people who have had multiple seizures (epilepsy), or are at risk of having multiple seizures. Identifying triggers and avoiding them is a must (avoiding sleep deprivation, bright / flashing lights, etc). Ketogenic diets have also been found to be beneficial in reducing seizure activity in some patients. Also, patients with epilepsy must know how to avoid certain activities in case they have a seizure while doing them (driving, climbing ladders, cooking with gas, stepping into bath tubs). If you see somebody that you suspect is actively seizing, the best thing to do is give them room, keep others back, and call 911. Do NOT try and hold them down, and do NOT stick anything in their mouth. It is a common misconception that people with seizures will swallow their tongue. This is physically impossible. Epilepsy is a very common neurologic disorder. Fortunately, we live in a time where we have so many different ways to treat seizures. New medicines are being invented all the time. Vimpat, for example, was just approved by the FDA 8 years ago, and is now used in hospitals all around the United States. We still have a long ways to go, but we're making great progress in treating epilepsy.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) is a Price-weighted index. That means that the index is calculated by adding up the prices of the constituent stocks and dividing by a constant, the "Dow divisor". (The value of the Dow divisor is adjusted from time to time to maintain continuity when there are splits or changes in the roster.) This has the curious effect of giving a member of the index influence proportional to its share price. That is, if a stock costing $100 per share goes up by 1%, that will change the index by 10 times as much as if a stock costing $10 per share goes up by the same 1%. Now look at the price of Google. It's currently trading at just a whisker under $700 per share. Most of the other stocks in the index trade somewhere between $30 and $150, so if Google were included in the index it would contribute between 5 and 20 times the weight of any other stock in the index. That means that relatively small blips in Google's price would completely dominate the index on any given day. Until June of 2014, Apple was in the same boat, with its stock trading at about $700 per share. At that time, Apple split its stock 7:1, and after that its stock price was a little under $100 per share. So, post-split Apple might be a candidate to be included in the Dow the next time they change up the components of the index. Since the Dow is fixed at 30 stocks, and since they try to keep a balance between different sectors, this probably wouldn't happen until they drop another technology company from the lineup for some reason. (Correction: Apple is in the DJIA and has been for a little over a year now. Mea culpa.) The Dow's price-weighting is unusual as stock indices go. Most indices are weighted by market capitalization. That means the influence of a single company is proportional to its total value. This causes large companies like Apple to have a lot of influence on those indices, but since market capitalization isn't as arbitrary as stock price, most people see that as ok. Also, notice that I said "company" and not "stock". When a company has multiple classes of share (as Google does), market-cap-weighted indices include all of the share classes, while the Dow has no provision for such situations, which is another, albeit less important, reason why Google isn't in the Dow. (Keep this in mind the next time someone offers you a bar bet on how many stocks are in the S&P 500. The answer is (currently) 505!) Finally, you might be wondering why the Dow uses such an odd weighting in its calculations. The answer is that the Dow averages go back to 1896, when Charles Dow used to calculate the averages by hand. If your only tools are a pencil and paper, then a price-weighted index with only 30 stocks in it is a lot easier to calculate than a market-cap-weighted index with hundreds of constituents. Sexual reproduction has some important advantages over asexual. DNA is prone to mutation, and if you just produced asexually, those mutations would carry on through your offspring forever (unless the mutation is reversed, which is highly unlikely). Sexual reproduction re-introduces the correct non-mutated gene back into the offspring which is called purging mutations. You also have the advantage of new couplings of genes, which allows for diversity. Diversity kind of gives natural selection some tools to work with when "building" new traits. Diversity is important in a changing environment (these changes are called selective pressures). Now as to why there are males and females as opposed to no gender, males have the advantage of quantity and females have the advantage of quality. Look at an egg cell vs a sperm cell. Eggs are large and you produce few of them (quality). You will likely nurture that one egg to success if it becomes fertilized. Look at a sperm cell. You expel about 200,000,000 per ejaculate (quantity). There are times when quantity becomes advantageous and times when quality becomes advantageous. So why be male or female? It is breeding season in your colony of seals. You, for some reason, get to choose to be a male or a female. There are very large scary males defending their groups of females (called a herem). Now, these males produce enough sperm (quantity) to fertilize every female egg. You cannot compete with them because you are too young (see elephant seals fighting). Now you could also choose to be female because you are guaranteed to pass on an offspring via your egg (quality). So in the case above, you could either be a male and try to fertilize a ton of females (might get none at all) or you could be a female and guarantee fertilization. Once upon a time people only had natural numbers: {0, 1, 2, 3, 4,...}. But then people were like "wait, we can do 3-2 = 1, but we can't do 2-3". So people invented the idea of negative numbers, so 2-3 = -1. Then, people were like "hey, we can do 10/2 = 5, but we can't do 2/10". So then people invented the idea of fractions, so 2/10 = 1/5. _ Then _, people were like "hey, we can do sqrt(25) = 5, but we can't do sqrt(-25)". So they invented the idea of imaginary numbers, so sqrt(-25) = 5i. Since this last part is the part you're likely confused about (ie, you understand how negatives and fractions work), a little more detail on how exactly the idea of imaginary numbers was invented. So first mathematicians said that there was this thing called i. And i has the property that i^2 = -1. (no other number that existed at that point had such a property). So then we get that sqrt(i^(2)) = sqrt(-1), or i = sqrt(-1). From this, we can define the squareroots of all negative numbers in terms of i. Ie, sqrt(-25) = sqrt(25\*(-1)) = sqrt(25)\*sqrt(-1) = 5i. However, unlike with negatives and fractions, where if we add two of them we'll get another number, with things involving i, it's not clear what something like 3 + 5i should be. So we just sort of define a new number called "3 + 5i" that can't really be written in any simpler way, just for the sake of having 3 + 5i be defined.

The clutch is located between the engine and the transmission and is operated by a pedal. When the pedal is pressed down, it disengages the clutch and disconnects the engine from the transmission. When the pedal is released, it engages the clutch and connects the engine to the transmission. Here's how it works: When you press down on the clutch pedal, it pushes a rod (called a throw-out bearing) that presses against a pressure plate. The pressure plate is a flat metal disk with a spring behind it. The spring is attached to the flywheel, which is a heavy metal disk that's attached to the back of the engine. When the pressure plate is pressed against the flywheel, it creates a gap between the two disks. This gap separates the engine from the transmission, which means the car can't move. When you release the clutch pedal, the spring behind the pressure plate pushes it back against the flywheel. This closes the gap between the two disks and allows the engine and the transmission to be connected again. The car can now move because power from the engine is being transferred to the transmission, which sends it to the wheels. The clutch is used when you want to shift gears or stop the car. First thing to remember is that language changes over time. It changes as it passes from generation to generation, and even over the course of your lifetime. No two people talk exactly the same. Family (parents) close friends, neighbors. In turn, they tend to sound like people they are closest to, including you. You get a large group of people, they will each have their own way of talking, but it will be fairly similar-it averages out, more or less. These tend to be geographical-people tend to sound like people they interact with a lot, which tends to be people they live near. So you've got a group of people who you interact with a lot, who live near you-this is a * dialect * or an * accent * (the main difference is, an accent is only how you pronounce words, a dialect also includes words you use that others don't. So the little changes accumulate, and the east side develops some that the west side hasn't, and vice versa. Soon, each side of town has a different dialect. Then say this process goes on for a long time. Each dialect keeps acquiring tiny changes. Pretty soon it gets hard for one group to understand the other. The more mass something has, the more force it feels from gravity (i.e. the more it weighs). However, the object's * inertia * (its resistance to being moved) increases with mass, as well. When an object is dropped, the increased force of gravity from its mass is exactly canceled out by the increased resistance to movement from its mass, and, all other things being equal (i.e. with no air resistance), all objects will fall at the same speed). * * * * * Here, have some math: Equation for gravitational force: F = (G \ * m*_1 _ * \ * m*_2 _ *) / r^(2) Equation for force from acceleration: F = m \ * a Let's mark which mass is the earth, and which is the object: F = (G \ * m*_object _ * \ * m*_earth _ *) / r^(2) F = m*_object _ * \ * a Now let's substitute the second equation into the first: m*_object _ * \ * a = (G \ * m*_object _ * \ * m*_earth _ *) / r^(2) Divide both sides by m*_object _ *: (m*_object _ * \ * a) / m*_object _ * = (G \ * m*_object _ * \ * m*_earth _ *) / (r^(2) \ * m*_object _ *) Cancel out m*_object _ * on each side: (~~m*_object_*~~ \ * a) / ~~m*_object_*~~ = (G \ * ~~m*_object_*~~ \ * m*_earth _ *) / (r^(2) \ * ~~m*_object_*~~) And we're left with: a = (G \ * m*_earth _ *) / r^(2) So the acceleration of an object on Earth (ignoring drag) depends only on the mass of the Earth, its distance from the Earth, and the gravitational constant, G. The mass of the object itself has no impact on its acceleration. * * * * * Bonus points if you noticed that I could just as have easily have written my second equation as: F = m*_earth _ * \ * a Remember Newton's laws, and the whole "for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction" thing? Well, not only is your object falling down toward the Earth, but * the Earth is also falling up toward the object *. This effect is so miniscule as to be effectively non-existant for objects with masses in the order of magnitude that you're used to interacting with, but if you want to be super technical, a more massive object will * technically * hit the ground first, because the ground will rise up to meet it faster.

The theory I subscribe to is this: Awareness of time's passage as fast (it seems to disappear) or slow (it seems to go forever) depends on * * how many times we notice things and notice ourselves noticing! * * Either can feel like a drag * or * fantastic depending on your circumstances. * * Time feeling slow:* * You watch a clock on the wall in class...10 minutes to the bell. Every...3...seconds, you observe how...* slow * it is. You want it to go faster, you wish it would, so you keep checking, again and again! In that 10 minutes you make * 200 observations *. And if every time you look at the clock you also say "That's so SLOW!" then that's * 400 observations * and it's even worse! It's like the clock...is in...slow...motion. Or think back to a day that was jam packed with incidents, 50 other kids on a field trip, where every comment and incident was important. At the end of the day, you are in bed remembering all the details of what happened that day-thousands of interesting things happened! Or recall the first time you bungy jump-time seems to slow down as your mind races through a dozen thoughts and lines of reasonings and self-assessments of how crazy you are, and who you love, and how you might die etc. And all in 3 seconds! (Other 3 second moments in your life don't even exist in comparison!) * * Time feeling fast * *: Now compare that to a day you just spaced out, not noticing anything at all, or a day half asleep in bed, or watching reruns of a TV series you know back to front. All of the sudden the day is gone. Or you are driving a route you've driven a thousand times-and suddenly you are home and you think, what the hell, was I sleep driving? -------------------------------------------- During childhood, there are things worth noticing all the time and little effort is required to discover them; everything in front of you is new so everything is important by that property alone. As you grow up, you stop noticing things you have seen a thousand times before-not new, not important and thus not worthy of your attention. It's normal and proper. As an adult, you need to make a conscious effort to find things that are worthy of your attention. Raw sensations / sights / sounds may not do it for you, unless they are extreme (time feels slower for thrill-seekers during genuine danger / risk and for wooing lovers who start paying attention to every detail). But generally, what is new / important for an adult is found on the abstract level (time slows for people who have jobs where every minute has a new-and important-challenges to overcome). -------------------------------------------------------------- As an aside note, two people could both live to 80, but the way they live their life could be really different. Maybe one is noticing things * all the time * - he's an inventor with a thousand observations and 100 ideas every day. The other spaces out completely and doesn't bother to remember anything. You could describe one person as having experienced 200 years worth of time, and the other as only having experienced 20 years worth!

Plaque can build up in the blood vessels over time and can eventually rupture, causing a blood clot to form. If the blood clot is large enough, it can block the blood flow to the heart, causing a heart attack. In some cases, heart attacks can be brought on by other factors, such as high blood pressure, smoking, or stress. However, they can also happen randomly, even in people who do not have any known risk factors for heart disease. It is also possible for people to have more than one heart attack. After a heart attack, it is important to work with a healthcare provider to make lifestyle changes and take medications as prescribed to lower the risk of having another heart attack.

A second passes, but time itself is not constrained by the tyranny of what a second is, the same as the concept of length itself is not constrained by meters or feet. Each moment is the now. You cannot subdivide the now, the now could be conceived of as the absolute smallest increment of time, kin to electrons or quarks (assuming, of course, nothing lies beneath * those *). Some key elements of computer architecture include: The instruction set architecture (ISA), which defines the commands that the computer's processor can execute and the format of the data it processesThe memory hierarchy, including the types and sizes of memory available to the system, such as main memory (RAM) and secondary storage (e.g., hard drives)The interconnections between the different components of the system, such as the bus that connects the processor to memory and the network that connects the computer to other devicesThe input/output (I/O) systems, which handle communication between the computer and external devices such as keyboards, mice, and printersUnderstanding computer architecture is important for designing and building efficient and effective computer systems, as well as for developing software that can take full advantage of the capabilities of the hardware.

It's always a good idea to have a retirement savings plan in place, no matter what your career path may be. Here are a few options to consider:401(k) plan: This is a retirement savings plan offered by many employers. Contributions are made through payroll deductions, and the funds in your account grow tax-deferred until you withdraw them in retirement. Individual Retirement Account (IRA): An IRA is a personal savings plan that you can set up on your own. There are two main types: traditional IRAs and Roth IRAs. With a Roth IRA, you contribute money that you've already paid taxes on, so the funds in your account grow tax-free and you can withdraw them tax-free in retirement. Pension: A pension is a retirement plan that is sponsored by an employer or union and pays a fixed amount to employees when they retire. Pensions are becoming less common, but if you have the option to participate in one, it can be a good source of income in retirement. Social Security: Social Security is a government-run program that provides a source of income for retired workers. The amount you'll receive in benefits is based on your earnings over your working years. No matter which option you choose, it's important to start saving for retirement as early as possible. The more time you have to save, the more your money has a chance to grow through compound interest. It's also a good idea to diversify your savings among different types of accounts to spread out your risk. Finally, be sure to review your retirement savings plan regularly to make sure it's still on track to meet your goals.

One of the main practices in Buddhism is meditation, which is a way of calming the mind and achieving greater awareness and understanding. Through meditation, Buddhists aim to develop concentration and insight, which can help them see the true nature of reality and end their suffering. Another important aspect of Buddhism is the concept of Karma, which is the idea that our actions and intentions have consequences that can affect our present and future lives. Buddhists believe that we can create positive Karma by acting with kindness, compassion, and understanding, and that this can lead to a better future. Overall, the goal of Buddhism is to achieve enlightenment, which is a state of perfect understanding and wisdom, and to use this understanding to help others. Buddhists believe that by following the path of mindfulness and compassion and by letting go of desire and attachment, we can find peace and happiness in this life and beyond.

A fuzzy system is a computational system that uses fuzzy logic, a mathematical logic that allows for uncertainty and imprecision in the form of partial truth values, to make decisions or predictions. Fuzzy systems are used in a variety of applications, including control systems, artificial intelligence, image processing, and data analysis. Fuzzy logic differs from classical Boolean logic, which represents values as either true or false, in that it allows for values to be partially true or false. This is represented by membership values, which can range from 0 to 1 and represent the degree to which a particular value belongs to a certain set or category. For example, a membership value of 0.7 for the set "hot" might indicate that a particular temperature is quite hot, while a membership value of 0.3 for the set "cold" might indicate that it is only somewhat cold. Fuzzy systems use fuzzy logic to process input data and make decisions based on that data. They typically consist of a set of rules that define how the input data should be processed, as well as a set of membership functions that map the input data to membership values. The output of a fuzzy system is typically a crisp value, which is a single value that represents the final decision or prediction made by the system. Fuzzy systems are often used in situations where there is a need to make decisions based on imprecise or incomplete data, or where there are multiple conflicting objectives that need to be balanced. They are particularly useful in control systems, where they can be used to stabilize processes or adjust system parameters in real-time.

I specialize in derivatives trading-mostly commodities based-so let me take a crack at this. Derivatives are derived from another asset that is their value is based on the value of something else. Lets use gold as an example. I commonly trade GLD which is an exchange traded fund(etf) for gold. It's much harder for a private(i.e. small, single person investor) to trade in the futures market(which is what gold is commonly traded as) than it is for you or I to buy a share of a company such as Apple(AAPL). There is some debate among traders, economist and the like whether the GLD ETF is a derivative, but I and many others would call it such given that with the exception of a few thousand tons of gold they own, there is no actual value for GLD other than what investors determine in the open markets. Derivatives do not grant you ownership in the way standard assets do. You don't get to vote about company leadership like you would if you owned stock. If your derivative is on Apple and they go bankrupt, you don't get money when they sell Steve Job's desk or iPhone. Options, futures and swaps are the most common derivatives. I'm not going to touch swaps, they're too complicated and without $100 M you're never going to trade them. Options are the ability to buy a certain asset(typically and for my purposes stocks such as GLD and AAPL) by a certain date at a certain price. Say GLD is trading at $169.00 today. You could buy an option for GLD that you would have to exercise by a certain date, say September 17th, 2011 at a certain price. An option to buy GLD on that date at a price of $170(the strike price) would cost you around $5. Almost all options contracts are in denominations of 100. So you'd actually be buying the right to buy 100 shares of GLD at $170 for $500. If you exercised your option and bought those 100 shares you would still have to pay 100*$170 of $17,000. But if the price of GLD went up to say $185 on September 14th per se, then you would pay $500 dollars to buy the option. Then on September 14th, you would pay $17,000 for the 100 shares, which would be valued at $18,500. Netting you a profit of $1000 after the $500 investment cost for the option contract. More commonly you would resell the option contract to actually realize your profit. The idea of the derivative is that as the value of the underlying entity increases, so does the value of the derivative. So on Sept. 14, your option contract would be worth more like $15 dollars and you would sell the contract to someone else, and never have to spend more than the initial $500. Derivatives are mostly used for the purposes of: (1) leveraging your money. That is if you had just purchased $500 worth of GLD and it went up to $185, you would have made just about $47 dollars or a healthy 9.46%, but not nearly the 200% you would have made with the option contract. Be mindful, however, that the opposite is true and that on September 17th, if your option contract is less than the strike price you bought you're contract is worthless. And most options contracts expire without value. Futures are similar to options, but do not have the option. If you bought a September 17th gold future on Sept. 17th you must take possession of the amount of gold the future was for at the price you agreed to when buying the future. This is true unless you sell the future contract to another trader. Futures are price predictors usually used by institutional investors. (2) Hedging on other investments. Say you owned an airline company. If the cost of gas were to go up dramatically, you would stand to lose a lot of money due to the increase in your overhead. To guard against this fear you could buy a option on gasoline for the future. If the price of gas went up dramatically, you would stand to gain a great deal of money from your option and decrease the lose from the increase in gas prices. If the cost of gas went down, then you'd only lose the minimal investment you made in the option but would profit from the decrease in your overhead. Sorry, I know this is long and not that clear, but it's the best I could do. I don't think any five-y - o would understand derivatives, it took me years of studying to get a minimal grasp on the subject. * * TLDR * * Derivatives are assets whose values is based on the value of another asset. If the underlying asset increases in value the derivative will also increase. And vice-versa. Derivatives don't have the asset backed element of most securities such as stock.

This would mean that people could use electricity without having to pay for the cost of building and maintaining power lines. In other words, Tesla's plan was to make electricity "free" in the sense that people wouldn't have to pay for the infrastructure needed to deliver it. Today, we do use electricity without having to pay for the infrastructure (like power lines) that delivers it to our homes and businesses. However, we still have to pay for the electricity itself, because it takes energy to produce electricity and that energy has a cost. So even if Tesla's idea had been successful, it would not have meant that electricity would be completely free. You would be surprised. Complex web servers are generally ran by an engineering team, which runs day to day operations. A development team is responsible for writing the actual code for the web site and it's various directories, pools, and extensions (essentially controlling what happens when you interact with the site). In order to test these items, staging or development servers are set up to first deploy these code packages to. Developers (as well as any non-security minded IT folks) don't understand and/or care about password requirements. They establish servers with 6-8 character passwords. When the code is deployed to the live system, these passwords are generally hardcoded into the code rather than changing the code, the engineering team changes their passwords to match. So now these various passwords are running as 6-8 characters. When a password is stored on a system, it is not stored as it looks (cleartext). Instead, it is hashed with a salt (a string of random characters). These hashes are then stored in a file, database, or some other media. When a password request is made, the system does the opposite--it uses the salt and derives the password from the hash. A complex system of password cracking uses a "rainbow table", which is a file that contains a massive amount of these hashes and compares the hash of the system to the hash in the rainbow table to find the password. This is the easiest way to crack passwords. However, web server vulnerabilities are not generally passwords. They are vulnerabilities in the server type (IIS, Apache, etc). Generally, live web servers are not patched immediately when the patch is released. Certain patches (specifically Microsoft patches) have a tendency to break web code. Larger companies lose a massive amount of money when the site is not accessible (certain sites like Amazon and eBay measure this by the second). Because of this, newer vulnerabilities can sometimes be exploited on large websites and access to the underlying server can be gained. Once there, it's simple to alter the website any way you like, or access various data directories or tables to download information. Finally, Anonymous employs certain database injection techniques to gather information from databases. These attacks are literally some of the easiest things a hacker can do. Websites generally have search options or forms that execute database queries on the underlying database server. When prompted for user entry, an SQL statement (database language) can be passed through this user input. If the programming team is not security conscious, the input will be passed as a query and the website will spit out any information requested. Almost everything is stored in databases and can be accessed like this. Credit card numbers, phone numbers, social security numbers, etc. Hope that helps.

Norwegian here. It's a Germanic language, descended from Norse and very closely related to the other Scandinavian languages (Swedish and Danish), to the point that being fluent in any of them means being at least conversant in all of them. In the Norse days we wrote with the Futhark much like then-close cousin Old English did, but now we write with an extended Latin alphabet: ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZÆØÅ Norwegian is a little strange in terms of written language because we have a long history of divisive language politics. This comes from the fact that the Norwegian * nation * is ~1000 years old but the modern Norwegian * state * is only ~100; we spent a lot of the intervening time being "ruled" more or less first by Denmark and then by Sweden. As such, we have one spoken language of many dialects but two written languages to write it down with: one that's based on Danish (called * bokmål *, literally' book language') and one that's reconstructed from the way Norwegian dialects are spoken around the country (called * nynorsk *, literally' New Norwegian'). The majority of Norwegians use bokmål primarily, and it rather dominates the media; there's constant debate about how much time schools and administration should devote to each of them. The difference between the two is mainly in vocabulary and spelling; grammar is pretty close. In terms of sentence structure we're fairly similar to Dutch or English-Germanic syntax but with word order taking on some of the job that cases used to do (or still do in other Germanic languages like modern German). Some dialects still have the full set of cases, but most have dropped some. Typical grammar nazi peeves include: * Confusing "og" (conjunction, equivalent to English "and") with "å" (infinitive marker, like the "to" in "to speak"), which sound fairly similar. * Writing compound words separated, which tends to totally change their meaning. * Misuse of apostrophes, primarily by imitation of English. Pretty much the only time it's correct to have an apostrophe in Norwegian is if you're writing the posessive form of a name ending in "s", "z" or "x", where they indicate that the possessive suffix -s is being omitted (e.g. "Sverres bil" for the car belonging to Sverre, but "Magnus' bil" for the car belonging to Magnus).

A common misconception is that the problem has to do with "hitting the system too hard". Like if you were trying to figure out where a truck was by slamming cars into it and listening for the crash: that will tend to push the truck around. Actually the problem is much more fundamental. Even a magical device that measured the position of an electron without bouncing any stuff off of that electron would disturb the state of the electron in a detectable way. Are you familiar with polarizers? When light moves, it waves back and forth. That waving has a direction. It can wave up and down (vertically), left and right (horizontally), diagonally, whatever. A polarizer is a grating that blocks light waving against the grating from passing through. It only lets light that's waving along the grating pass through. But something interesting happens when light waving * diagonally * to the grating is passed through a polarizer. The light is partially let through, and * afterwards will be waving along the grating's direction *. You can use a polarizer to figure out how some unknown light is polarized. Pass the light through the polarizer and see how much light is let through as you turn the polarizer. Assuming the light doesn't contain a mix of polarizations, there will be a direction that lets all the light through. That's the polarization of the light. But suppose you don't have a beam of light. You have just a single photon. You want to figure out its polarization. Now the pass-it-through-polarizers-at-various-angles idea won't work so well. Even if the photon survives the first polarizer, its polarization is forced to wave along with the grating. The photon's polarization may have been diagonal to the grating beforehand, but not anymore. So a second polarizer can only tell us about the first polarizer's orientation, instead of about the photon's original polarization. In quantum mechanics, measurements behave like polarizers. You can use a measurement to split photons into a horizontally-polarized group and a vertically-polarized group, but doing so will force diagonally polarized photons to be horizontally or vertically polarized. Even worse, there's fundamentally no way to make the groupings finer: any process that splits photons into horizontal, vertical, and diagonal groups will be unreliable. All of this can be proven from the mathematical postulates of quantum mechanics. That's what physicists mean when they say that measurement changes a system in quantum mechanics: 1. The system can occupy a continuum of states, but measurement can only give discrete ("quantized") results. 2. Further measurements only tell you about the previous measurement instead of about the system's original state. 3. Thus measurement forces systems "diagonal" to a measurement to be "along-or-against" that measurement, unavoidably affecting them.

The assumption that house value appreciates 5% per year is unrealistic. Over the very long term, real house prices has stayed approximately constant. A house that is 10 years old today is 11 years old a year after, so this phenomenon of real house prices staying constant applies only to the market as a whole and not to an individual house, unless the individual house is maintained well. One house is an extremely poorly diversified investment. What if the house you buy turns out to have a mold problem? You can lose your investment almost overnight. In contrast to this, it is extremely unlikely that the same could happen on a well-diversified stock portfolio (although it can happen on an individual stock). Thus, if non-leveraged stock portfolio has a nominal return of 8% over the long term, I would demand higher return, say 10%, from a non-leveraged investment to an individual house because of the greater risks. If you have the ability to diversify your real estate investments, a portfolio of diversified real estate investments is safer than a diversified stock portfolio, so I would demand a nominal return of 6% over the long term from such a diversified portfolio. To decide if it's better to buy a house or to live in rental property, you need to gather all of the costs of both options (including the opportunity cost of the capital which you could otherwise invest elsewhere). The real return of buying a house instead of renting it comes from the fact that you do not need to pay rent, not from the fact that house prices tend to appreciate (which they won't do more than inflation over a very long term). For my case, I live in Finland in a special case of near-rental property where you pay 15% of the building cost when moving in (and get the 15% payment back when moving out) and then pay a monthly rent that is lower than the market rent. The property is subsidized by government-provided loans. I have calculated that for my case, living in this property makes more sense than purchasing a market-priced house, but your situation may be different.

Memorizing a grocery list is hard when the items have nothing to do with each other. But it's easier if they do. If you're a baker, and you need to go get flour, sugar, butter, and eggs, it's pretty easy to remember that list because they're the 4 basic baking ingredients. But if the list is 3 yellow onions, a quart of half-and-half, toothpaste, and dog food, it's going to be really easy to forget something. That's the key to memorization. Your brain can really only hold on to so many things at once (I've heard 7 as an upper limit), so to memorize more you have to chunk things together into one thing. If I could only remember one thing, I could memorize the first list as "the 4 basic baking ingredients" and the second with some kind of memory device: "I need to brush the dog's teeth with onions cooked in half-and-half". Lines in a movie or play are memorized by becoming so familiar with the scene that it's just one thing. Rather than "I have to say this sentence, then wait for her to say hers, then say this next sentence..." it just becomes "do the scene". Amateur actors take a lot of repetitions to get there, while veteran actors can get there quicker by visualizing the whole thing in their head and "mentally rehearsing" it before the actual rehearsal.

Quantitative easing, or QE, is a monetary policy tool that central banks, such as the Federal Reserve in the United States, use to try to stimulate economic growth. When a central bank engages in QE, it buys government bonds from banks and other financial institutions, using money that it creates out of thin air. This increases the amount of money that these financial institutions have available to lend to businesses and consumers, which can help to boost economic activity. One reason that QE may not lead to inflation is that banks may not necessarily lend out all of the money that they receive from the central bank. Instead, they may choose to hold onto some of the money as a precaution against potential future economic downturns. This means that the extra money created through QE may not make its way into the broader economy as quickly as it might in normal times. Another reason is that during times of economic downturn, when QE is typically used, there is often a lot of spare capacity in the economy, such as idle factories and high unemployment. This means that businesses may not have the ability or the demand to produce and sell more goods and services, even if they have access to more money to do so. Without an increase in demand for goods and services, there is little reason for businesses to raise prices, and therefore little risk of inflation. It's important to note that QE is just one of many tools that central banks can use to try to influence the economy, and its effects can vary depending on the specific circumstances of a given situation.

This has already been answered fairly well, but just to fill out the historical context: Back in the day, floppy drives were your primary storage media, and hard drives were expensive and uncommon peripherals. You would keep your operating system on a floppy disk, and boot from that disk when you turned on your computer. Then you would switch disks to your program and load that afterwards. Yes, you literally installed your OS every time you turned the computer off. Did I mentioned hard drives were expensive? There were so expensive that people would put up with this shit rather than buy them. Fancy computers would have * two * disk drives. That way you could boot from one floppy, and have a program disk in the other drive, without having to switch disks. Software assumed that the first drive was the floppy drive that contained the OS, which was labeled A. Secondary floppy drives were more common than hard drives, so if there was a B drive it was obviously a floppy drive. If you had a hard drive, you didn't want to confuse programs into thinking it was a disk drive so you labeled it C to avoid ambiguity. It was not until later that hard drives were considered normal. Many of the programs on those hard drives were written in the preceding years and were still generating business value, so the drive lettering was kept around to appease their quirks with minimum fuss. The islands of Ireland and Great Britain were first unified under one Crown in the Acts of Union 1801, forming the "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland." English attempts to extend its sphere of influence into Ireland, however, date back many centuries. Ireland, being the most remote and culturally independent nation-state of the British Isles, was the last nation (after Wales and Scotland) to submit to English rule. In 1919, after a century of political union, Ireland revolted against the British government and successfully established the "Irish Free State" in 1922. Initially, the entire island of Ireland was ceded by Britain, but the region now known as Northern Ireland, being more hospitable to British rule than the rest of Ireland, immediately exercised its right to rejoin the political union. The sovereign state, the "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland" was thusly incorporated and exists in the same capacity today. The "Republic of Ireland" was formed in 1937, succeeding the Irish Free State. There have been various insurgencies and periods of unrest in the region, primarily Northern Ireland, over the century of Ireland's independence. This has been highlighted by the so-called "Troubles," starting in the 1960s and spanning the rest of the century. It was an ethnic and political struggle where Catholic Irish republicans (who supported secession from the UK and union with the Republic of Ireland) combatted Protestant Irish / English unionists (who supported remaining in union with the UK). A patchwork of various ceasefires and agreements have brought about an uneasy peace. The conflict is largely political now, having lost its military aspect, and concerns the status of Northern Ireland--whether it should remain a part of the UK or join the rest of Ireland. Primary factors fueling the conflict are: historical grievances (the English didn't exactly treat the Irish with warmth), religious differences (primarily Protestant Britain and primarily Catholic Ireland), ethnicity and probably most importantly, Irish nationalism.

Keeping things ELI5 as much as possible: C4 has energy stored in the form of chemical bonds. Those bonds release energy in the form of heat when they are broken, in addition to converting the solid C4 into a gas (which takes up a lot more space). If this happens all at once (or at least very quickly), you get what you would define as an explosion: Lots of heat and pressure in a single small point, which expands very quickly as a shockwave. If this happens slowly, it's more like a traditional fire: Heat and gas separate off of the burning mass at a rate (which is actually controlled by how quickly the substrate heats up in the presence of its own fire). C4 does not require oxygen to burn so as it heats up the fire intensity will increase. So to answer your question, you have to understand that there are two ways to break the bonds in C4. A significant impact (~~a bullet~~ apparently probably not a bullet, but definitely a priming charge) will do the trick, and so will heat. The heat permeates the C4 slowly, resulting in a fire. The shockwave from a priming charge however permeates the entire mass very quickly, releasing all the bonds at once: Boom.

The question is complicated because there's overlap. Gasoline is primarily used in vehicles, propane is primarily used as a portable cooking / heating / lighting fuel, and natural gas is used as a stationary cooking / heating / water heating / electricity generation fuel. We prefer gasoline in cars because it's generally safer than a tank of compressed or liquified gas in your car. Yet, some vehicles burn propane. We prefer propane as a portable camping / outing fuel, but "white" gasoline can be used for all the same purposes. But white gasoline requires a bit of compressed air in the tank to push it along (the user pumps up the tank a few times with a built-in air pump) and likely needs to be converted to an aerosol (mist) as well. But propane, a liquified gas, "pumps itself," making propane-fueled equipment less complex. The propane boils off into its gaseous state as the tank empties, so you can use every last bit of it from the tank. No pump needed. Natural gas, like gasoline, is relatively cheap. But like propane, it is compressed (just not to the point of liquification, most of the time), so it does not need to be pumped. I don't know why they don't typically liquify natural gas, but not liquifying it certainly makes it inconvenient for portable applications.

A pilot study is a small-scale research project that aims to test the feasibility, design, and potential outcomes of a larger study. It is usually conducted before the main research project in order to identify any issues that may arise and to make necessary changes to the design or methodology before proceeding. Pilot studies are commonly used in the fields of medicine, psychology, and social sciences, but they can also be conducted in other fields such as engineering, education, and business. They may involve collecting data from a small sample of participants, conducting a small-scale experiment, or testing a new measurement tool or intervention. Pilot studies are useful for determining whether a larger study is likely to be successful and for refining the study design. They can also provide valuable information about the factors that may influence the results of the main study, such as participant characteristics, sample size, and measurement techniques.

Variable rate loans can be a good option for some borrowers, but they may not be the best choice for everyone. It's important to carefully consider the potential risks and benefits of a variable rate loan before deciding if it is the right choice for you. One potential benefit of a variable rate loan is that the interest rate may be lower than the interest rate on a fixed rate loan. This can result in lower monthly payments and potentially save you money over the life of the loan. However, it's important to keep in mind that the interest rate on a variable rate loan can also increase over time, which could result in higher monthly payments. If you are considering a variable rate loan, it's a good idea to consider the following factors: Your financial stability: If you have a stable income and a good credit score, you may be better equipped to handle the potential fluctuations in monthly payments that can come with a variable rate loan. Your risk tolerance: If you are comfortable taking on more risk in exchange for the potential for lower payments, a variable rate loan might be a good option for you. However, if you prefer the security of knowing exactly what your monthly payments will be, a fixed rate loan might be a better choice. The terms of the loan: Make sure you understand the terms of the loan, including how often the interest rate can change and what factors can cause the rate to change. This will help you better understand the potential risks and benefits of a variable rate loan. Overall, it's important to carefully consider your financial situation and risk tolerance before deciding if a variable rate loan is the right choice for you.
